content:
"Does Islam accept religious pluralism?" sounds like one question, and it is at least five. People who ask it may mean whether Islam accepts that many religions exist, whether it protects their followers, whether it talks with them, whether it holds them all true, or whether it says they can be saved.

The answers differ, and running them together produces two false slogans: that Islam calls every religion equally true, and that Islam has no place for anyone outside it.

This article aims to provide context to the question, insha'Allah, in five distinctions, each drawn from the Quran and its commentators. The Quran's own statement of diversity frames them: "To each among you have we prescribed a law and an open way. If Allah had so willed, He would have made you a single people, but (His plan is) to test you in what He hath given you: so strive as in a race in all virtues" (5:48).[1]

The Quran states that God made mankind into many communities, and that He could have made them one (5:48). It also calls itself the guardian of the scripture before it, "confirming the scripture that came before it, and guarding it in safety" (5:48).[1]

The same verse holds both: the many communities are God's will for this world, and the revelation that judges between them is one. Accepting that religions differ commits a Muslim to nothing about whether their claims are true. The Quran makes claims that contradict others, chief among them that God is one and has no son.

"Allah forbids you not, with regard to those who fight you not for (your) Faith nor drive you out of your homes, from dealing kindly and justly with them" (60:8). Mankind was made "into nations and tribes, that ye may know each other" (49:13).[1]

Al-Fārūqī described a pax Islamica in which Jews, Christians and others lived under their own law.[2] Its ground is the Quran's rule: "Let there be no compulsion in religion" (2:256).[1] Muslims can defend the rights of their neighbours without saying that their neighbours' creeds are true. We set out the Quran's rules for friendship in can a Muslim befriend a non-Muslim?

The Quran invites the People of the Book to "common terms as between us and you: That we worship none but Allah" (3:64), and tells Muslims to argue with them only "with means better (than mere disputation)" (29:46).[1] The common ground is real, and so is the disagreement.

Al-Fārūqī called this kind of tolerance a "scholarly investigation of the genesis and development of the religions", which separates "the historical accretions from the original given of revelation".[3] Dialogue in that sense is a disciplined argument between people who take truth seriously. We set out the Quran's rules for the call in principles of daʿwah in the Quran.

Quran 2:62 promises reward to "those who believe (in the Qur'an), and those who follow the Jewish (scriptures), and the Christians and the Sabians,- any who believe in Allah and the Last Day, and work righteousness".[1] Quran 3:85 says: "If anyone desires a religion other than Islam (submission to Allah), never will it be accepted of him."[1]

Ibn Kathīr records Ibn ʿAbbās's view that 3:85 came after 2:62, and reads the two together: before Muhammad (peace be upon him), "every person who followed the guidance of his own Prophet was on the correct path", and after his mission, only what conforms to his law is accepted.[4] Joseph Lumbard reads the inclusive verses more widely, while granting that most Muslim scholars read the exclusive ones restrictively.[5] Mun'im Sirry has traced how modern interpreters contest the exclusivist reading.[6] We set out the verses and the classical readings in does the Quran send every non-Muslim to hell?

A doctrine of what God accepts does not tell a Muslim the fate of any particular person. The Quran says that God does not punish until He has sent a messenger (17:15), and that leaves open who has truly been reached, and how.[1]

Mohammad Hassan Khalil's study of the question, Islam and the Fate of Others, shows how widely the great Muslim theologians differed on it.[7] Judgement belongs to God, and the believer's task is to invite.

The bottom line

Islam accepts that many religions exist and calls that diversity God's will. It commands justice and kindness to peaceful neighbours of every faith, invites them to common terms, and argues with them in the better way. None of this makes every religion true. The Quran's claim to truth stands, and its scholars have read its verses on salvation in more than one way.

The word "pluralism" hides those distinctions; the Quran keeps them. Every person is born upon "the standard Religion", "the pattern on which He has made mankind" (30:30), and the invitation to it is made freely and with justice.[1] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Quran 5:48; 60:8; 49:13; 2:256; 3:64; 29:46; 2:62; 3:85; 17:15; 30:30, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  2. Ismail R. al Faruqi, Essential Writings, ed. Imtiyaz Yusuf (Leesburg, Va.: Center for Islam in the Contemporary World, and Petaling Jaya: Islamic Book Trust, 2021), "The Islamic World Order: Pax Islamica", pp. 192–193.
  3. Ismāʿīl Rājī al-Fārūqī, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life, 2nd ed. (Herndon, VA: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 1992), chapter 4, section IV.
  4. Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm, on Quran 2:62, abridged English translation on quran.com.
  5. Joseph Lumbard, "Qur'anic Inclusivism in an Age of Globalization", Iqbal Review, October 2005.
  6. Mun'im Sirry, "Contesting the Theology of Exclusivist Salvation", in Scriptural Polemics: The Qur'an and Other Religions (New York: Oxford University Press, 2014).
  7. Mohammad Hassan Khalil, Islam and the Fate of Others: The Salvation Question (New York: Oxford University Press, 2012).
